title: Strings — std::string and std::string_view
summary: `std::string` **owns** its text and can change it. `std::string_view` is a cheap, read-only **window** onto text that lives somewhere else. Functions that only read text should take a `std::string_view`.
markdown:
## A string is a row of characters ``` std::string name{ "Hello" }; index: 0 1 2 3 4 ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ │ H │ e │ l │ l │ o │ name.length() is 5 └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ name[0] is 'H' name[4] is 'o' ``` Each character has a position, called its **index**. Counting starts at **0**, so the last index is always the length minus one. > [!danger] Stay inside the string > `name[5]` on a five-character string reads past the end. That is undefined behaviour. The compiler will not stop you. ## Calling a string's own functions A `std::string` comes with functions attached. You call them with a dot after the variable: `name.length()`. Functions attached to a value like this are called **member functions**. ```cpp #include #include int main() { std::string first{ "Ada" }; std::string last{ "Lovelace" }; std::string full{ first + ' ' + last }; std::cout << full << " has " << full.length() << " characters\n"; // 12 std::cout << "Initials: " << first[0] << last[0] << '\n'; // AL std::cout << "Surname starts at index " << full.find(last) << '\n'; // 4 return 0; } ``` ## The toolbox Assume `std::string s{ "Hi" };` for each row. | To | Write | Result | |---|---|---| | Get the length | `s.length()` | `2` | | Get one character | `s[0]` | `'H'` | | Join two strings | `s + " there"` | `"Hi there"` | | Add to the end | `s += "!";` | `s` is now `"Hi!"` | | Compare | `s == "Hi"` | `true` | | Check for empty | `s.empty()` | `false` | | Find text | `s.find("i")` | `1` | | Take a piece | `s.substr(0, 1)` | `"H"` (start index, how many) | | Insert | `s.insert(0, ">> ")` | `">> Hi"` | | Remove | `s.erase(0, 1)` | `"i"` (start index, how many) | | Replace a piece | `s.replace(0, 1, "Oh")` | `"Ohi"` | Converting between text and numbers: | To | Write | Result | |---|---|---| | Number to text | `std::to_string(42)` | `"42"` | | Text to `int` | `std::stoi("42")` | `42` | | Text to `double` | `std::stod("3.5")` | `3.5` | > [!note] When `find` finds nothing > It returns a special value, `std::string::npos`. Always compare the result against it before using it as an index: > ```cpp > if (s.find("x") == std::string::npos) { /* not there */ } > ``` > [!warning] `"Hello" + " World"` does not compile > Text in quotes is a **string literal**, which is a more primitive thing than a `std::string`. The `+` only joins when at least one side is a real `std::string`: write `std::string{ "Hello" } + " World"`. ## `std::string_view`: look, do not copy Passing a `std::string` to a function copies the whole text, as with any other argument. For long text that is wasted work when the function only wants to read it. A `std::string_view` holds no text of its own. It records **where** some existing text is and **how long** it is. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["std::string
owns: Hello, World"] --- V1["string_view
sees: Hello, World"] S --- V2["string_view
sees: World"] ``` ```cpp #include #include #include void greet(std::string_view name) { std::cout << "Hello, " << name << '\n'; } int main() { greet("Ada"); // works with a literal std::string s{ "Grace" }; greet(s); // works with a std::string, without copying it return 0; } ``` | | `std::string` | `std::string_view` | |---|---|---| | Owns the text | Yes | No | | Can change the text | Yes | No | | Cost of passing it to a function | Copies every character | Tiny: a location and a length | | Use it for | Text you store or modify | **Parameters that only read** | > [!danger] A view must not outlive what it looks at > ```cpp > std::string_view broken() > { > std::string temp{ "oops" }; > return temp; // temp is destroyed here; the view now points at nothing > } > ``` > A view is only valid while the text it refers to still exists. This idea, something referring to data that has gone, returns in Milestone 4 under the name **dangling**. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does `std::string{ "banana" }.find("na")` return? - `3` - `1` + `2` - `true` > `find` returns the index where the first match begins. Counting from 0, `b`=0, `a`=1, `n`=2. ? When should a function take a `std::string_view`? - When it needs to store the text for later - When it needs to change the caller's text + When it only needs to read the text, not store it or change it - Whenever the text is longer than 100 characters > A `std::string_view` looks at existing text without copying it. It cannot change the text, and it must not outlive the string it views. ? What does `find` return when the text is not there? - `-1` - `0` + `std::string::npos` - The length of the string minus one > `find` returns the special value `std::string::npos` when there is no match. `0` would mean a match at the very start. ? What is the index of the last character of a string of length 8? + `7` - `8` - `9` - `0` > Indexes start at 0, so a string of length 8 has indexes 0 to 7. Index 8 is one past the end. ```
ideas:
1. Read a full name. Print the first name, the last name, the initials and the total length, using `find(' ')` and `substr`.
2. Replace the first `"cat"` in a sentence with `"dog"` using `find` and `replace`.
3. Write `void printBoxed(std::string_view text)` that prints the text with a `*` on each side.

cards.a:
`2`

`find` returns the index where the first match begins. Counting from 0, `b`=0, `a`=1, `n`=2.

cards.q: When should a function take a `std::string_view`?
cards.a:
When it only needs to read the text, not store it or change it

A `std::string_view` looks at existing text without copying it. It cannot change the text, and it must not outlive the string it views.

cards.q: What does `find` return when the text is not there?
cards.a:
`std::string::npos`

`find` returns the special value `std::string::npos` when there is no match. `0` would mean a match at the very start.

cards.q: What is the index of the last character of a string of length 8?
cards.a:
`7`

Indexes start at 0, so a string of length 8 has indexes 0 to 7. Index 8 is one past the end.
